extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical political philosophy; readers of Plato's Republic
extracted.subtask_short: Plato Republic: regimes and character types
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt from Plato's Republic describing the characteristics, defects, and origins of oligarchy, democracy, and tyranny, and the corresponding individual character-types (the oligarchical man, the democratic man, the tyrant). Useful for analyzing regime-types and moral psychology in classical political theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oligarchy: qualification by property as defect
rubrics_metrics.description: If pilots (or rulers) are chosen according to their property, and a poor but better pilot is refused permission to steer, the government is defective; qualification by wealth displaces competence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original worry: choosing rulers by wealth leads to incompetence and 'shipwreck' of the common enterprise. Anti-pattern: allowing property rather than merit to determine offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oligarchy: bifurcation into rich and poor ('two States')
rubrics_metrics.description: An oligarchical State is not one but two States—the one of poor, the other of rich men—living on the same spot and always conspiring against one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence: chronic internal division and conspiracy between classes; instability and lack of unity are endemic to oligarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oligarchy: incapacity for effective warfare and tax reluctance
rubrics_metrics.description: Oligarchies are often incapable of carrying on war: either they arm the multitude and then fear them, or they keep them unarmed and have too few to fight; their love of money makes them unwilling to pay taxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical defect: military weakness and fiscal stinginess undermine state security and public goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oligarchy: citizens performing too many callings
rubrics_metrics.description: Under oligarchy the same persons have too many callings—they are husbandmen, tradesmen, warriors, all in one—giving a poor appearance and unhealthy division of labor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation: social roles blurred; lack of specialization and dignity in occupations is a sign of disorder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oligarchy: extremes of wealth and poverty; non-participating paupers
rubrics_metrics.description: Oligarchies have both extremes of great wealth and utter poverty; a man may sell all he has and remain dwelling in the city yet no longer partake in active citizenship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Result: many citizens become paupers in proximity to wealth, not full members of civic life—this signals deep social injustice and instability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drone analogy: stingless and stinging drones as social pests
rubrics_metrics.description: The drone in the house is like the drone in the honeycomb: some drones are made without stings (paupers) and others with dreadful stings (criminals). 'Of the stingless class are those who in their old age end as paupers; of the stingers come all the criminal class.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnostic: presence of paupers and hidden thieves/robbers indicates systemic moral and educational failure; lawgiver should guard against producing drones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oligarchy: lack of education and ill-training produces malefactors
rubrics_metrics.description: The existence of criminals in such States is attributed to want of education, ill-training, and an evil constitution of the State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy implication: education and proper civic training are essential to prevent crime and degeneration in oligarchies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oligarchical individual: avaricious/miserly character
rubrics_metrics.description: The oligarchical or avaricious man values wealth highly, is penurious and laborious, satisfies only necessary appetites, saves from everything, and is applauded by the vulgar; he is not a man of cultivation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Psychological profile: enforced virtue (coercion by fear of loss) rather than cultivated goodness; moral weakness manifests when entrusted with others' property (e.g., guardianship of an orphan).

rubrics_metrics.name: Oligarchical individual: coerced virtue and divided soul
rubrics_metrics.description: He coerces bad passions by enforced virtue—necessity and fear constraining them—so his natural desires of the drone exist whenever he has to spend what is not his own. He is 'two men' at war with himself; better desires generally prevail but the true unity and harmony of soul flee from him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral evaluation: externally enforced restraint is inferior to internal cultivation; such a person lacks the 'unanimous and harmonious soul' of true virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oligarchy→Democracy transformation mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Oligarchy tends to produce widespread carelessness and extravagance; rulers refuse to curtail spendthrift youth because they profit by their ruin (buying estates), leading to many of good family reduced to beggary and ready for revolution. The poor, once armed or empowered, may conquer and institute democracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Causal chain: economic exploitation breeds resentment and revolution; political short-term profiteering by elites undermines regime stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedy proposed: voluntary contracts 'at his own risk'
rubrics_metrics.description: One suggested remedy is a general rule that everyone shall 'enter into voluntary contracts at his own risk', which will lessen scandalous money-making and reduce the evils occasioned by oligarchy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy guidance: legal/contractual reforms encouraging personal responsibility can mitigate exploitative money-making practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy: freedom, variety, and election by lot
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracy arises when the poor have conquered and give an equal share of freedom and power; magistrates are commonly elected by lot. The city is full of freedom and frankness—one may say and do what one likes—and contains the greatest variety of human natures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterization: democracy is 'like an embroidered robe spangled with every sort of flower'—its variety is both attractive and disorderly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy: disregard for cultivation and promotion of popular friends
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracy tramples underfoot fine notions of cultivation and promotion of qualities that make a statesman; it promotes to honour any who profess to be the people's friend, valuing popularity over education and statesmanship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical assessment: democratic promotion of popularity over competence can degrade civic norms and public prudence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic individual: origin and character (democratic man)
rubrics_metrics.description: The democratic man often arises from the oligarchical upbringing but, after tasting unnecessary pleasures and associating with libertine associates, becomes varied in tastes: he alternates between pleasures, politics, athletics, philosophy, and business; he lives 'from day to day', terms his disorderly life 'joy and bliss', and treats all pleasures as alike.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Psychological profile: lacks order and stable hierarchy of desires; values freedom and equality of pursuits, resulting in an undisciplined and motley life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary vs unnecessary pleasures distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Necessary pleasures are those we cannot get rid of, which benefit and are essential (e.g., simple food for health); unnecessary pleasures are those of which a man may get rid (delicacies, luxuries) and which often harm body and soul and are hurtful to wisdom and virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative standard: moral education should train youth to shun unnecessary pleasures and restrain appetites that undermine virtue and the life of wisdom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy's excess of liberty leads to anarchy and erosion of respect
rubrics_metrics.description: Excess of freedom breeds anarchy: children level with parents, masters flatter scholars, slaves are as free as their purchasers, sexes equal in relation, animals treated as free—citizens become sensitive, impatient of touch of authority, and cease to care for laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnosis: boundless liberty corrodes authority, respect, and lawfulness, setting the stage for tyranny as a corrective reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class structure in democracy facilitating tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracy divides into three classes: (1) drones (leaders and busybodies), intensified in democracy and managing public speech, (2) the wealthy class (orderly, squeezable, source of revenue), and (3) the people who work with their hands (largest class). The drones incite redistributions while reserving benefits for themselves, creating a root for tyranny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanism: class manipulation and demagogic exploitation of envy and ignorance enable rise of a 'protector' who becomes tyrant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protector→Tyrant transition (mechanism and tactics)
rubrics_metrics.description: A people's protector appears as champion, uses false accusations, murders or banishes opponents, hints at abolishing debts and distributing lands to win support, then requests a bodyguard ('Let not the people's friend be lost to them'), forms a paid and trusted band, and converts into a tyrant who purges the able and wealthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequence to watch for: popular champion gains power through promises and emergency measures, then institutionalizes personal rule via bodyguard and purges. Anti-patterns: empowering a protector without safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tyrant's methods for maintaining power
rubrics_metrics.description: The tyrant keeps the people impoverished by stirring wars and extracting taxes so they remain dependent and distracted; he must eliminate valiant, high-minded, wise, and wealthy persons (a 'purgation' that removes the better part) and surrounds himself with satellites whom he pays and who are often drones or freed slaves enrolled as bodyguard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: tyranny requires constant manufacture of enemies, wars, purges, and a loyal, paid retinue; the regime's survival rests on repression and economic deprivation of subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of poets and tragedians in relation to tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragic poets (e.g., Euripides) eulogize tyranny; they attract mobs, gain honours (greatest from tyrants, next greatest from democracies), and can help draw cities toward tyrannies and democracies by persuasive speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultural note: poets and rhetoricians can legitimize and promote tyrannical tendencies; the lawgiver should be aware of cultural influencers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lawgiver/physician metaphor: remove drones early
rubrics_metrics.description: The good physician and lawgiver ought, like the wise bee-master, to keep the drones at a distance and prevent their coming in; if they have entered, he should have them and their cells cut out speedily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preventative policy: identify and exclude parasitic classes (drones) early through institutional design and education to preserve civic health.
